method: solved independently, every answer re-verified in sympy (exact solve/expand/limit/minimum, not arithmetic by hand); option sets scanned programmatically for sum/product/multiple/square/sign-flip relations

SAM11-01.note: f(5)=40, f(1)=0, 40/4=10. Single-step definition recall; medium at most. Distractor family is the denominator error set: 40 = forgot to divide, 8 = divided by 5 (endpoint count) instead of 4, 20 = divided by 2. STRUCTURE: key 10 is the hub - 20=2x10, 40=4x10, 40=5x8. Not backsolvable (key is a derived rate, not a value you can test in the stem).
SAM11-01.trap_leak: weak - 40/10/8 form a visible 'wrong denominator' ladder, so a student who knows only that the interval has length 4 picks 40/4 without computing f at all; that is still the intended arithmetic though.

SAM11-02.note: L+2w=60, Lw=400 -> w^2-30w+200=0 -> w=10 (L=40) or w=20 (L=20, a square). The clause 'the side parallel to the wall is longer' rejects w=20. Exclusivity rests ENTIRELY on that one clause; without it both 10 and 20 are defensible and both are options. It is fair, but it is the only thing standing between this item and a double key.
SAM11-02.backsolve_detail: w=40 gives negative L (out), 6.67 gives area 311 (out), 10 and 20 both give area 400 - two tests, then the clause. Faster than the quadratic.
SAM11-02.trap_leak: moderate - the tie-break sentence is a meta-tell. An author only writes it when both roots are legal, so 'the smaller perpendicular side' is indicated before any algebra; 10 and 20 are the adjacent pair and 10 is the one that makes the clause true.
SAM11-02.structure: key 10 is the hub: 20=2x10, 40=4x10. 6.67 is the isolated option.

SAM11-03.note: (2x-3)^3 = 8x^3 - 36x^2 + 54x - 27. Routine binomial expansion. 54 is the x-coefficient (read the wrong term), -18 halves the 3-choose-1 count, 36 is the sign flip.
SAM11-03.trap_leak: weak - the (-36, 36) sign pair brackets, and 54 is visibly the neighbouring coefficient, so a solver who expands only the sign gets to two options. Still needs the 3*(2x)^2*(-3) term.
SAM11-03.structure: -36 = 2x(-18), 36 = -(-36), 54 = -3x(-18): all four sit in one family generated by -18.

SAM11-04.note: u=sqrt(x): u^2-5u+6=0, u=2,3, x=4,9, both check, sum 13. Good hard-route item: the bait is Vieta read off the printed equation, which gives 5, and 5 is an option. 6 is the u-product, 9 is one solution.
SAM11-04.trap_leak: moderate - 5 and 6 are transparently the u-equation's Vieta pair and 9 is transparently a single root, so a student who merely knows 'the answer is not the sum-of-u trap' is left with 13 by elimination without ever finding x=4. The three distractors are all labelled by their own arithmetic.
SAM11-04.structure: no arithmetic relation among any pair; all four isolated.

SAM11-05.note: g = -x^2+6x+2, vertex x=3, g(3)=11. Equivalently min f = -4, so max(-f) = 4, +7 = 11. Medium.
SAM11-05.trap_leak: MODERATE - 11 and 4 differ by exactly 7, the constant printed in the stem. The option set therefore displays the final step of the intended method, and the trap taxonomy ('forgot to add 7') names the larger as the key. A student who knows only that a shift of +7 is the last step picks the top of the pair. 3 (the vertex x) and 2 (g(0)) are not competitive.

SAM11-06.note: p=(x-3)^2(x-r), constant -9r=18 -> r=-2, p = x^3-4x^2-3x+18, a=-4. Note -3 is exactly b, the OTHER constant in the same expansion - a well-chosen distractor. 2=-r, 4=-a.
SAM11-06.trap_leak: weak-moderate - (4, -4) is a sign pair and -3 is recoverable as b, so the set is 'the three numbers this expansion produces plus a sign flip'. A solver who expands at all sees -4 and -3 together and must decide which the stem asked for; that is the item working as intended.
SAM11-06.structure: 4 = -(-4) = 2^2 = 2x2; -3 is the isolated option (and the isolated-option heuristic picks it, wrongly).

SAM11-07.note: (3-x)/(3x) / (x-3) = -1/(3x). Options are a clean 2x2 factorial on sign and on the factor of 3 - no option is built from another and nothing leaks structurally.
SAM11-07.backsolve_detail: ONE substitution kills it: x=1 gives (1-1/3)/(1-3) = -1/3, which matches only -1/(3x). The intended common-denominator step is never performed. This is the cheapest substitution win in the batch.
SAM11-07.trap_leak: none - a genuinely clean option set.

SAM11-08.backsolve_detail: testing options against 5x+6=15 is the same work as solving; a calculator student can evaluate all four directly. Backsolve is available but not faster.

SAM11-09.note: xz = 3y^2+1 -> y = sqrt((xz-1)/3), positive root by y>0. Clean 2x2 factorial (sign of 1, and whether the 3 divides inside or the whole). Standard literal-rearrangement item, not hard route.
SAM11-09.backsolve_detail: pick y=1, x=1, so z=4; the four options evaluate to sqrt(7/3), sqrt(1/3), sqrt(5/3), 1. Only the key returns 1. No algebra. This is the canonical 'plug in numbers' item and every prepped student does it this way.
SAM11-09.trap_leak: none - the option set itself is clean; the exposure is the item type.

SAM11-10.note: x-y=3, x^2+y^2=65 -> (7,4) for positive values. STRONGEST WITH-STEM LEAK IN THE BATCH.
SAM11-10.trap_leak: STRONG - zero algebra is required. The stem says 'two positive numbers', which deletes -4. 28 is impossible because 28^2 alone exceeds 65 - a one-glance plausibility kill. That leaves 4 and 7, which are exactly the two numbers of the answer pair, and the stem asks for the GREATER, so the answer is 7. The item hands over both members of its own solution pair and then tells the solver which one to take. A student who cannot solve a system of two equations still scores this.
SAM11-10.structure: 28 = 4*7 = the product of the two survivors; 4 = -(-4).

SAM11-11.note: equal degrees, ratio of leading coefficients 6/2=3. Single-fact recall, the easiest item in the batch alongside SAM11-12. 2.5 = 5/2 (wrong coefficients), 0 = the deg(num)<deg(den) case, -6 unmotivated.
SAM11-11.backsolve_detail: evaluate f(1000) on the calculator: 3.0. Takes seconds and needs no asymptote concept at all - the 'increases without bound' phrasing invites exactly this.
SAM11-11.trap_leak: weak - -6 is the only option with no derivation and reads as filler.

SAM11-12.note: 2y^3=54 -> y=3. Easy; would be a module 1 item. 27=y^3, 6=x, 18=6x3.
SAM11-12.backsolve_detail: y=3 -> x=6 -> 6*9=54. One line, faster than the cube root.
SAM11-12.trap_leak: weak - 27 is visibly 3^3 and 6 visibly 2x3, so both distractors advertise themselves as intermediate quantities and leave 3 as the only terminal value. Weakened by 18 being unmotivated.

SAM11-13.note: remainder theorem at the root of 2x-1: p(1/2) = 1/2+2-3/2+5 = 6 (sympy division confirms quotient 2x^2+5x+1, remainder 6). The non-monic divisor is the hard-route twist. 14 = p(1), i.e. divided by x-1 instead - the exact named error. 5 = p(0).
SAM11-13.trap_leak: moderate - 14 = 9+5 and 5 is the constant term, so 5 and 14 are both recognisable as 'wrong evaluation point' answers; a student who knows the divisor is non-monic eliminates the x=1 and x=0 products and is down to 9 or 6.
SAM11-13.structure: 14 = 9+5; key 6 is the isolated option (the isolated-option heuristic picks it correctly here - one of only 3 hits in 9 firings, i.e. noise).

SAM11-14.note: (x-4)(2x+1) = 2x^2-7x-4; times (x+3) gives x-coefficient -21-4 = -25 (sympy: 2x^3-x^2-25x-12). Mechanical expansion, error-prone but not conceptually hard - medium.
SAM11-14.trap_leak: MODERATE - -21 is precisely 'found one of the two cross terms', -12 is the constant term of the same product, -1 is the x^2 coefficient. Three of four options are the OTHER coefficients of the very polynomial being expanded, so any student who expands even partially sees several of their own intermediate numbers listed and knows the key is the one they have not yet accounted for. The set is a coefficient inventory.
SAM11-14.structure: no arithmetic relations; all four isolated.

SAM11-15.note: (8+2w)(10+2w)=168 -> w^2+9w-22=0 -> w=2 (rejecting -11). Very standard border problem. 11 = |negative root|, 4 = 2w, 12 = 10+2 or the framed width.
SAM11-15.backsolve_detail: w=2 -> 12x14 = 168. One multiplication. Also note 4 -> 16x18 = 288 and 12 -> 32x34, both instantly out, so the field is really 2 vs 11 and 11 gives 30x32.
SAM11-15.trap_leak: moderate - the (2, 4) factor-of-2 pair is the classic 'border width vs total added width' bracket, and the stem's 'width, in inches, of the border' resolves it to the smaller. 11 is the rejected-root marker. Elimination on taxonomy alone gets a student to 2.

SAM11-16.note: vertex at x=5 lies OUTSIDE [0,3]; f decreases on the interval so the least value is f(3) = -3 (f(0)=18 is the max). sympy minimum over Interval(0,3) confirms -3. Best-designed item in the batch: -7 = f(5), the exact unconstrained-vertex trap; 5 = the vertex x-coordinate; 18 = the endpoint that is the maximum.
SAM11-16.trap_leak: moderate - a student who merely recognises 'restricted domain' knows -7 is the bait and that the answer is an endpoint value; f(0)=18 and f(3)=-3 are both present, and 'least' plus the visible negativity points at -3. Even so, deciding which endpoint requires knowing the vertex is to the right, which is the intended reasoning. I would keep this item unchanged.
SAM11-16.structure: no arithmetic relations; all four isolated.

SAM11-17.note: R = p(80-2p), vertex at p=20, R=800. Medium. 20 = the optimal price (answered the wrong quantity), 1600 = 80x20 (dropped the -2p), 1200 unmotivated.
SAM11-17.trap_leak: weak-moderate - 20 is a UNITS outlier: three options are in the hundreds/thousands and one is a price. A solver who finds p=20 and sees it listed knows it is the bait for the wrong quantity. 1600=2x800 brackets. The real dilution is 1200, which has no derivation.
SAM11-17.structure: 1600 = 2x800 (key is the base of the pair).

SAM11-18.note: zeros 3/2, 3, -4; sum 1/2. Medium. Two of the four options (-4 and 1.5) ARE zeros of p - the 'gave a root instead of the sum' family. 2.5 is unmotivated.
SAM11-18.trap_leak: moderate - once the zeros are found, two of them are sitting in the option list, which confirms the factorisation is right and makes the addition the only remaining step. Cheap reassurance rather than a leak, but it removes the possibility of a silent factorisation error.
SAM11-18.structure: key 0.5 is the hub: 1.5=3x0.5, 2.5=5x0.5. Note 1.5 is both a zero and 3x the key - dual role.
SAM11-18.duplicate_flag: shares its skill with SAM11-06 and SAM11-14 (polynomial in factored/expanded form, extract one number).

SAM11-19.note: f(2)=f(6) puts the axis at x=4, so 7 and 1 are equidistant from it and f(7)=f(1)=0. sympy solve gives f = -x^2+8x-7, f(7)=0. Genuine hard-route item and the only one in the batch that rewards a structural insight over computation - the symmetry route needs no coefficients at all.
SAM11-19.trap_leak: weak - 9 is the vertex value k, -7 is the constant term C, -16 is unmotivated. A student who solves the system sees 9 appear and must not stop there.
SAM11-19.caution: 0 as a key in a numeric set is slightly conspicuous - it is the only option a guesser reads as 'special'. Does not change my grade.

SAM11-20.note: 16^(3/4)=8, x^8->x^6, y^-4 -> y^-3 = 1/y^3. Clean 2x2 factorial on the coefficient (2 vs 8) and the sign of the y exponent - no option built from another, no taxonomy leak. Medium.
SAM11-20.backsolve_detail: two substitutions fully decide it. x=y=1 gives 16^(3/4)=8, killing both '2' options; then x=1,y=2 gives (16/16)^(3/4)=1, which matches 8/y^3 = 1 and not 8y^3 = 64. Exponent rules never invoked.

SAM11-21.note: 240/n - 240/(n+4) = 2 -> n^2+4n-480=0 -> n=20 (rejecting -24). Check 12 vs 10, difference 2. Well-constructed as a free-response item; as four-choice it is largely given away.
SAM11-21.backsolve_detail: test n=20 in one line. Also every distractor is testable in one division.
SAM11-21.trap_leak: STRONG, second only to SAM11-10 - solvable from the stem's wording plus option arithmetic with no equation at all. 10 and 12 are dollar amounts (240/24 and 240/20) and differ by exactly the 2 dollars named in the stem; 20 and 24 are people-counts differing by exactly the 4 new members named in the stem. So the set is transparently {share now, share later, members now, members later}. The stem asks for members NOW, which is the smaller of the person-pair: 20. A solver who only matches the numbers 2 and 4 in the stem to the gaps in the option set arrives at the key without writing anything.
SAM11-21.structure: 20=2x10, 24=2x12 - all four options lie in two parallel doubling pairs.

SAM11-22.note: 3g-4 = 6x^2+5 -> g = 2x^2+3. Medium. 2x^2+1/3 divides only the wrong term, 2x^2+9 forgets to divide the 9, 18x^2+19 applies f instead of its inverse.
SAM11-22.backsolve_detail: x=0 decides it in one step: f(g(0))=5 forces g(0)=3, and only one option has constant 3. The quadratic term is never examined. Three seconds.
SAM11-22.trap_leak: weak - the three distractors differ from the key only in the constant, so the item is effectively a one-number question and the substitution above answers it.

SAM11-23.note: isolate and square: 6 = 2sqrt(x), x=9; sqrt(16)-sqrt(9) = 1. Unique solution, no extraneous root to discard, which costs the item most of its difficulty.
SAM11-23.backsolve_detail: 9 is the only option for which BOTH x and x+7 are perfect squares (9 and 16). Testing it is one glance; testing the others requires a calculator and fails immediately (36 -> 6.56-6, 18 -> 5-4.24, 29 -> 6-5.39). The batch's most mechanically backsolvable item.
SAM11-23.trap_leak: weak-moderate - the 'both are perfect squares' property is visible before any work and is a recognised test-wise cue on radical items.

SAM11-24.note: two distinct real solutions requires k^2-100 > 0, so k > 10 and the least positive integer is 11. The strict inequality is the whole item and it is a correct, classic module-2 twist. 10 is the double-root boundary, 100 = the discriminant constant, 5 = sqrt(25).
SAM11-24.backsolve_detail: compute the discriminant for each option: only 11 and 100 give a positive value, and 100 is not least. Two evaluations.
SAM11-24.trap_leak: MODERATE-STRONG and worth the author's attention - 10 and 11 are ADJACENT integers, which is itself the announcement that the boundary is excluded. A student who computes k^2 > 100 but is unsure whether the endpoint counts simply observes that the item would be pointless if 10 were the key (why print 11?) and takes 11. Separately, 5, 10 and 100 form one derivational family (10=2x5, 100=10^2) and 11 is the lone outsider - the only option that is not a round number, in a question whose phrase 'least possible positive integer' promises a non-round answer.
SAM11-24.structure: 10=2x5, 100=10^2=10x10; key 11 isolated - the clearest odd-one-out in the batch. Reported as structure per the bank-wide finding that hub/outlier patterns run at or below chance.
